title: Wal-Mart, the discount chain from small-town Arkansas
what: Wal-Mart Stores, run by its founder Sam Walton from Bentonville, Arkansas, sells everyday goods at low prices in small towns of the American South. It has grown from 38 stores and 44 million dollars of sales when it went public in October 1970 to 276 stores and about 21,000 employees in 1979, and its yearly sales are about to pass one billion dollars. The Walton family owned 61% of the shares at the listing.
why: The starting point of one of the great compounding stories of the game: at the start a player can buy a fast-growing regional chain that will become the largest retailer in the world. Game-start beat (the stock was listed long before the game begins).

title: Wal-Mart passes a billion dollars in yearly sales
what: Wal-Mart's sales for the business year that ended on 31 January reached about 1.25 billion dollars, against 44 million in 1970. No retailer has reached the billion-dollar mark so fast. In 1977 Forbes ranked it first among discount retailers for return on equity and for growth in sales and earnings.
why: Establishes the growth engine that drives the stock through the 1980s. The exact publication month of the annual figures is not confirmed; April is the month the annual report would normally be out.

title: Wal-Mart agrees to take over the Kuhn's Big K chain
what: Wal-Mart agreed in June to buy Kuhn's Big K, a struggling discount chain, in a deal valued at about 13 million dollars. The purchase brings 92 stores and pushes Wal-Mart into the Southeast. A first attempt to merge the two in 1980 had failed over store leases.
why: The first sizeable acquisition, and the start of the expansion out of the home region that fed the 1982-83 rerating.

title: Retail stocks lead the new bull market
what: Since the Federal Reserve cut its discount rate in mid-August, share prices have surged, with record trading of 149 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange on 4 November. Shares of retailers that sell to consumers are among the biggest winners as investors bet on falling interest rates and a recovery in spending.
why: Wal-Mart's +21% in November (market +4%) came in the middle of a rally in which consumer retailers led; no Wal-Mart-specific news for that month was found, so the beat explains it as part of the sector move. Wal-Mart's best twelve months in the game run from 1982-07 to 1983-07 (+201%).

title: Sam Walton dances the hula on Wall Street
what: On 15 March Wal-Mart's chairman Sam Walton, 65, danced the hula in front of Merrill Lynch on Wall Street with a Hawaiian band, keeping a promise to his employees. He had bet they could not lift the company's pre-tax profit to 8% of sales in 1983. They did.
why: Colour for the culture behind the margins: Wal-Mart made high profits on low prices, which is what investors were paying for.

title: Forbes: Sam Walton is the richest man in America
what: Forbes magazine's new list of the 400 richest Americans puts Wal-Mart founder Sam Walton at the top, with an estimated 2.8 billion dollars, almost all of it in Wal-Mart shares. The Walton family holds 54 million shares. Wal-Mart has about 750 stores in 19 states and expects sales of about 6.2 billion dollars this year.
why: Shows how far the share price had come: the family fortune is the stock. The UPI report is dated 10 November 1985 and says the list came out the week before; PBS dates the list to October 1985.

title: Black Monday hits the high-flyers hardest
what: On Monday 19 October the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 508 points, or 22.6%, its worst day ever. Wal-Mart shares had already dropped 11.7% on Friday 16 October. Stocks that had risen most, such as Wal-Mart, were among the hardest hit; on 20 October the Federal Reserve promised to supply cash to the banking system.
why: Wal-Mart's worst stretch in the game, -41% from 1987-08 to 1987-11. The business did not change; the price of growth did, and it recovered within two years.

title: The first Wal-Mart Supercenter
what: This year Wal-Mart opened its first Supercenter, in Washington, Missouri: a discount store and a full supermarket under one roof. It follows the Hypermart USA experiment, a giant store opened near Dallas in 1987. Wal-Mart is now the most profitable retailer in the United States.
why: The Supercenter became the growth vehicle of the 1990s and made Wal-Mart America's largest grocer. The opening month is not confirmed, so the beat sits at the end of the year.

title: Wal-Mart reaches California and the billion-dollar profit
what: Wal-Mart opened its first stores in California this year and now trades from coast to coast. Its US sales have roughly quadrupled since 1985 to about 32 billion dollars. In 1989 it became the first retailer to earn more than one billion dollars after tax in a year, with 1,402 stores and 272,000 employees.
why: The national roll-out that made Wal-Mart number one; the stock rose about 35% in 1990. Opening month in California not confirmed, so the beat sits at year end.

title: Wal-Mart overtakes Sears as America's largest retailer
what: Sears reported 1990 sales of 31.99 billion dollars for its stores business, knocking it off the top spot it had held since about 1900. Wal-Mart, with 1990 sales of 32.6 billion dollars, is now the country's largest retailer, and Kmart, at 32.07 billion, also passed Sears.
why: The defining milestone of the first decade: the small-town chain is number one. The stock had risen about tenfold since the start of the game.

title: Wal-Mart goes abroad, starting in Mexico
what: In 1991 Wal-Mart formed joint ventures with Cifra, Mexico's largest retailer. The first store, a Club Aurrera warehouse club in Mexico City, opened late this year. Wal-Mart also launched its own label, Sam's American Choice.
why: The start of the international business that later brought Canada, Germany, Britain, Japan, India and losses as well as growth. The beat sits in the month of the big +20% move but does not explain it; see Unexplained moves.

title: Wal-Mart enters Canada with 122 Woolco stores
what: Wal-Mart is buying 122 Woolco stores in Canada from Woolworth, for about 335 million dollars, and will convert them to its own name. Last year it bought 91 Pace warehouse clubs from Kmart. Growth at home is slowing as Wal-Mart reaches most of the country.
why: The mid-1990s were Wal-Mart's flat years on the stock market; growth had to come from new formats and new countries.

title: Wal-Mart opens in China
what: In August Wal-Mart opened a Supercenter and a Sam's Club in Shenzhen, China; about 80,000 people came on the first day. Wal-Mart already trades in Mexico and Canada and is looking for growth abroad as growth at home slows.
why: Part of the international push of the flat mid-1990s; the stock was roughly where it had been in 1992.

title: Wal-Mart joins the Dow Jones Industrial Average
what: On 17 March Wal-Mart replaced Woolworth in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, alongside Hewlett-Packard, Johnson & Johnson and Travelers, which replaced Westinghouse, Texaco and Bethlehem Steel. Wal-Mart's yearly sales have passed 100 billion dollars.
why: A symbolic changing of the guard (the old five-and-dime leaves, the discounter enters) and the start of a run in which the stock rose about fivefold by the end of 1999.

title: Wal-Mart is the best stock in the Dow
what: Wal-Mart shares have about doubled in 1998, after rising some 70% in 1997, making it the best performer in the Dow Jones Industrial Average this year. Comparable-store sales are growing faster than last year, and the company bought back about 1.2 billion dollars of its own shares.
why: The late-1990s rerating, when investors paid internet-like multiples for steady growth. Chief executive David Glass himself warned in the annual report that such gains were 'unusual'.
source: Wal-Mart Stores 1999 Annual Report, letter and Q&A with David Glass, https://stock.walmart.com/_assets/_46796feebc5ddf6d2adbeabac9558ae9/walmart/db/950/9626/annual_report/1999-annual-report-for-walmart-stores-inc_130199459840185623.pdf (read 2026-10-03); https://corporate.walmart.com/news/2008/11/06/wal-mart-reports-october-1998-sales (search result summary read 2026-10-03)

title: Wal-Mart buys Britain's Asda for 10.8 billion dollars
what: On 14 June Wal-Mart agreed to pay 6.7 billion pounds, about 10.8 billion dollars or 220 pence a share in cash, for Asda, Britain's third-largest supermarket chain. Its offer trumped a merger planned with the British retailer Kingfisher, which withdrew. Asda's board recommends the bid.
why: Wal-Mart's biggest foreign bet; it made Wal-Mart the world's largest retailer and was sold in 2021 at roughly the same value in pounds.

title: David Glass steps down; Lee Scott takes over
what: In January David Glass stepped down as Wal-Mart's president and chief executive and was succeeded by Lee Scott, who had run merchandising and logistics. Glass stays on the board. Wal-Mart's yearly sales are now about 165 billion dollars.
why: The handover coincided with the top of the stock: it peaked around the turn of the millennium and did not close a year above the end-1999 level again until 2013. The CNN report of 14 January could not be opened; the date comes from the search result summary of it.

title: Wal-Mart tops the Fortune 500
what: Wal-Mart heads Fortune magazine's list of America's largest companies for the first time, with revenue of 219.8 billion dollars, the first service company ever to lead the list. Last year it also became the largest grocer in the country.
why: Peak size and peak scrutiny; the stock itself was stuck in a range from 2000 to about 2011. PBS dates the list to 7 June 2002; Fortune usually publishes it in the spring, so the month is approximate.

title: Judge allows sex-discrimination suit for 1.6 million women
what: A federal judge in San Francisco has certified a class action against Wal-Mart on behalf of about 1.6 million women who have worked in its US stores since late 1998. They claim they were paid and promoted less than men. Wal-Mart denies it and will appeal.
why: The largest employment class action in US history hung over the stock for seven years, part of the image problems of the 2000s (wages, unions, local opposition to new stores).

title: Wal-Mart gives up on Germany
what: On 28 July Wal-Mart said it will sell its 85 German stores to the rival Metro and leave the country, taking a loss of about one billion dollars. Vice chairman Mike Duke said it had become clear that Wal-Mart could not reach the scale and results it wanted there.
why: The clearest failure of the international strategy begun in 1997 with the Wertkauf purchase.
source: https://www.forbes.com/2006/07/28/walmart-germany-metro-cx_po_0728walmart.html (search result summary read 2026-10-03); https://www.cbsnews.com/news/wal-marts-german-flop/ (search result summary read 2026-10-03)

title: Shoppers flock to Wal-Mart as the crisis deepens
what: Wal-Mart's US comparable-store sales rose 2.4% in October while many retailers report falling sales. 'We see more customers shopping more often at Walmart,' said the head of its US stores, adding that a family of four can save 700 dollars a year on groceries there. Falling petrol prices should help its customers into the holidays.
why: The defensive side of the stock: Wal-Mart's share price rose about 18% in 2008 while the market lost about 40%.

title: Wal-Mart cuts its profit forecast after a hard Christmas
what: On 8 January Wal-Mart said the holiday season was 'more challenging for retailers than expected'. US comparable sales rose only 1.7% in December, and it cut its forecast for quarterly earnings to 91 to 94 cents a share from 1.03 to 1.07 dollars, citing the strong dollar and lawsuit settlements. Customers are focused on necessities.
why: Even the recession winner was not immune; the shares fell 16% in January, about twice the market's fall.

title: Supreme Court throws out the giant discrimination suit
what: On 20 June the US Supreme Court ruled that the women suing Wal-Mart for sex discrimination cannot proceed as a single class of about 1.5 million, because their claims do not share a common question. All nine justices agreed the class was improper.
why: Removes a large legal overhang that had hung over the stock since 2004.

title: New York Times: Wal-Mart hushed up bribery in Mexico
what: The New York Times reported on 21 April that Wal-Mart de Mexico paid more than 24 million dollars in bribes to win permits for new stores, and that headquarters shut down its own investigation without telling the authorities. Shares of the Mexican unit fell 12% on the Monday after the report.
why: A reputational and legal blow to the international business; investigations ran for years.
source: https://abcnews.go.com/blogs/business/2012/04/wal-mart-de-mexico-engaged-in-widespread-bribery-nytimes-reports (search result summary read 2026-10-03); https://money.cnn.com/2012/04/22/news/companies/walmart-mexico-bribery/index.htm (search result summary read 2026-10-03)

title: Doug McMillon to become Wal-Mart's chief executive
what: On 25 November Wal-Mart announced that Doug McMillon, head of its international business, will replace Mike Duke as chief executive on 1 February 2014. He will be the company's fifth chief executive.
why: McMillon led the costly turn to higher wages and online shopping, which first hurt the stock (2015) and then rerated it (2020s).

title: Wal-Mart warns profits will fall; shares drop 10% in a day
what: On 14 October Wal-Mart said earnings per share will fall 6 to 12% next year, mainly because it is spending 1.5 billion dollars on higher pay, raising its minimum wage from 9 to 10 dollars an hour, and investing in online shopping and lower prices. The shares fell 10% to 60.03 dollars, their worst day in more than 17 years, wiping out almost 20 billion dollars of market value.
why: The low point of the McMillon reset; the stock lost about 29% in 2015 and then recovered as the investments paid off.

title: Wal-Mart buys Jet.com to fight Amazon
what: On 8 August Wal-Mart agreed to buy the online retailer Jet.com for 3.3 billion dollars. Jet's founder Marc Lore will lead Wal-Mart's US online business, which is growing far more slowly than Amazon.
why: The start of Walmart's serious e-commerce push, the theme behind the rerating of the 2020s.

title: Now Walmart Inc., the shares slide on slower online growth
what: From 1 February the company is called Walmart Inc. instead of Wal-Mart Stores. On 20 February its shares fell about 10% after holiday-quarter profit came in below forecasts (1.33 dollars a share against 1.36 expected) and US online sales grew 23%, after 50% the quarter before.
why: Profit-taking after a 43% gain in 2017; the market judged Walmart by its online growth now.

title: Walmart pays 16 billion dollars for India's Flipkart
what: On 9 May Walmart agreed to buy 77% of Flipkart, India's largest online retailer, for 16 billion dollars, beating Amazon to the deal. It is the biggest acquisition in Walmart's history.
why: A bet on the fastest-growing large consumer market; investors worried about the cost at first.

title: Pandemic shoppers stock up at Walmart
what: Walmart reported that in the three months to April net sales rose 11% and online sales 74%, as Americans stocked up during the coronavirus lockdowns. Customers came less often but bought 16.5% more per visit, and profit rose 4% despite higher costs.
why: The pandemic proved Walmart's stores could double as an online delivery network; the stock gained about a fifth in 2020.

title: Inflation squeezes Walmart; worst day since 1987
what: On 17 May Walmart reported quarterly earnings of 1.30 dollars a share against 1.48 expected, and said full-year profit would now fall about 1% instead of rising. Higher fuel and wage costs and swollen inventories ate into margins. The shares fell 11.4%, their worst day since 16 October 1987.
why: Inflation hit the low-price model before it helped it; the stock recovered within a year as better-off shoppers traded down to Walmart.

title: Walmart announces a three-for-one stock split
what: On 30 January Walmart announced a three-for-one split of its shares, its first in 25 years, so that employees can more easily buy them. Shares will trade on the new basis from 26 February.
why: Housekeeping (the prices in the game are split-adjusted), but it opens a year in which the stock rose about 70%.

title: Walmart buys Vizio after a year of big gains
what: In December Walmart completed its 2.3 billion dollar purchase of the television maker Vizio, to sell more advertising on screens in people's homes. Walmart's shares have risen by about 70% this year, as its online shop, advertising and membership businesses grow.
why: The 2024 rerating: investors began to value Walmart partly as a technology and advertising platform, not only a grocer.

title: McMillon to retire; Walmart moves to Nasdaq
what: On 14 November Walmart said chief executive Doug McMillon will retire at the end of January and be succeeded on 1 February by John Furner, head of Walmart U.S., who joined as an hourly worker in 1993. On 20 November it announced it will move its share listing from the New York Stock Exchange to Nasdaq in December, the largest such switch on record.
why: Orderly succession at the top of the market; the Nasdaq move underlines how Walmart now presents itself as a technology company.

title: John Furner takes over a trillion-dollar Walmart
what: John Furner became Walmart's president and chief executive on 1 February. In February Walmart became the first traditional retailer to be valued at more than one trillion dollars. It employs about 2.1 million people, more than any other private company.
why: Where the arc stands today: from a regional chain at the start of the game to one of the most valuable companies in the world.
